candidates.label: A
candidates.abstract: Byte-addressable persistent memory allows ordinary stores to update nonvolatile data, but crash recovery still requires permissible persistence order. Enforcing that order by waiting for durability at every epoch boundary can couple execution to persistence completion. We introduce WHISPER, a suite of ten applications spanning direct persistence, transactional libraries, and file-system access, and use its traces to motivate the Hands-Off Persistence System (HOPS). Most durable transactions contain 5–50 epochs; same-thread epoch conflicts are common, whereas cross-thread conflicts are uncommon in the measured traces. Persistent accesses average 3.54% of memory accesses in the simulated subset, placing persistence support within a machine dominated by volatile traffic. HOPS separates ordering from completion: ofence closes an epoch without demanding synchronous durability, while dfence waits when durability is required. Per-thread Persist Buffers retain updates and multiple versions, with dependency metadata preserving necessary order. Full-system gem5 simulation of a four-core out-of-order x86 machine reports a 24.3% performance improvement over x86-64 clwb plus sfence with durability at NVM, and 10% over the x86-64 Persistent Write Queue configuration. A subset of WHISPER runs to completion. These gains require buffers, metadata, and cache/coherence changes; cross-thread conflicts still need handling, and conservative tracking can introduce false dependencies. Aggregate chip area and power remain unverified.
introduction: Persistent memory combines byte-addressable nonvolatile storage with ordinary memory instructions, but that access interface does not remove the need for crash recovery. Persistent stores must survive in an order that leaves a recoverable state, even as applications continue to use volatile DRAM. An epoch groups persistent stores between ordering points; completing an epoch's ordering obligations and completing its durability need not be the same event. Persistent-memory software spans interfaces exemplified by Mnemosyne [volos2011mnemosyne] and PMFS [dulloor2014pmfs], so an architectural proposal needs evidence beyond a single access style. We construct WHISPER from ten applications covering direct persistence, transactional libraries, and file-system access, including native key-value/database systems, library-backed stores, and PMFS-backed services. Programs are adapted for recovery and instrumented, and Eliza extracts their persistent-access traces.

WHISPER exposes a reason to separate ordering from synchronous completion. Most durable transactions contain between 5 and 50 epochs, and Echo and the N-store TPC-C workload can exceed a hundred. Same-thread epoch conflicts are common, so ordering cannot simply be discarded; cross-thread conflicts are uncommon in the measured traces, suggesting value in retaining per-thread persistence state while still handling dependencies across threads. In the simulated subset, persistent accesses average only 3.54% of memory accesses. This measured mix motivates persistence support that allows execution to proceed amid predominantly volatile traffic. HOPS implements this separation through Buffered Epoch Persistency: ofence ends an epoch without requiring synchronous durability, and dfence waits for durability where the program needs it, such as transaction completion. Per-thread Persist Buffers retain persistent updates and multiple versions while dependency metadata preserves the necessary order. The interface therefore lets an application express when order is required separately from when persistence must have completed.

We evaluate HOPS using gem5 full-system Linux simulation of a four-core out-of-order x86 machine, with a subset of WHISPER running to completion. Each hardware thread has a 32-entry Persist Buffer, and background flushing begins at 16 entries. Against x86-64 clwb plus sfence with durability reached at NVM, HOPS without persistent write queues improves performance by 24.3%; it also outperforms the x86-64 Persistent Write Queue configuration by 10%. An ideal comparison ignores ordering and therefore does not provide crash consistency; it is not an implementable persistence baseline with equivalent guarantees. HOPS obtains its reported gains by adding per-thread storage, retained versions, dependency metadata, and cache/coherence changes, for which no verified aggregate chip-area or power result is available. Rare cross-thread conflicts remain part of the correctness problem, and conservative dependency tracking can create false positives. The contribution is thus a workload-grounded separation of ordering and completion, with performance benefits demonstrated for the simulated application subset and explicit architectural costs still to account for.

candidates.abstract: Byte-addressable persistent memory permits ordinary memory instructions to update nonvolatile storage, but recoverable applications still need to order those updates. Requiring durability at every ordering point can couple execution to completion more tightly than recovery requires. We study this distinction through WHISPER, ten applications spanning direct persistence, transactional libraries, and file-system access, with persistent-access traces extracted by Eliza. Most durable transactions contain 5–50 epochs; same-thread epoch conflicts are common, whereas cross-thread conflicts are uncommon in the measured traces. In the simulated application subset, persistent accesses average 3.54% of memory accesses, placing persistence support within a machine dominated by volatile traffic. HOPS implements Buffered Epoch Persistency by separating ordering from durability: ofence ends an epoch, while dfence waits for durability when required. Per-thread Persist Buffers retain updates and multiple versions, and dependency metadata preserves necessary ordering. Full-system gem5 evaluation of a four-core out-of-order x86 machine uses 32-entry buffers with background flushing at 16 entries. For the evaluated subset, HOPS without persistent write queues improves performance by 24.3% over clwb plus sfence with durability at NVM, and exceeds the x86-64 persistent-write-queue configuration by 10%. These benefits require buffering, versioning, and cache/coherence changes; uncommon cross-thread conflicts still need handling, and conservative dependency tracking can introduce false positives.
introduction: Persistent memory changes how software reaches nonvolatile data, but it does not remove the need for crash recovery. Applications can issue ordinary loads and stores to byte-addressable storage while continuing to use volatile DRAM. Recoverability depends on which persistent updates may survive together and in what order. An epoch groups persistent stores between ordering points, making the relationship between order and completion central to architectural support. Software approaches include persistent-memory libraries and file systems, represented by Mnemosyne [volos2011mnemosyne] and PMFS [dulloor2014pmfs]. Understanding their application behavior is necessary to determine when persistence support must constrain execution and when updates can remain buffered.

WHISPER assembles ten applications spanning direct persistence, transactional libraries, and file-system access. The programs are adapted for recovery and instrumented, and Eliza extracts their persistent-access traces. Most durable transactions contain 5–50 epochs, although Echo and the N-store TPC-C workload can exceed a hundred. Same-thread conflicts between epochs are common; cross-thread conflicts are uncommon in these traces, but remain possible. In the simulated application subset, persistent accesses average only 3.54% of memory accesses. Together, these observations motivate support that preserves dependencies across epochs while allowing persistence completion to proceed separately from ordering. HOPS provides that separation through Buffered Epoch Persistency: ofence closes an epoch without demanding synchronous durability, and dfence waits for durability at points such as transaction completion. Per-thread Persist Buffers retain persistent updates and multiple versions, with dependency metadata recording the order that must be preserved.

We evaluate HOPS using gem5 full-system Linux simulation of a four-core out-of-order x86 machine, running a subset of WHISPER to completion. Each hardware thread has a 32-entry Persist Buffer, with background flushing triggered at 16 entries. HOPS without persistent write queues improves performance by 24.3% over x86-64 clwb plus sfence when durability is reached at NVM, and outperforms the x86-64 Persistent Write Queue configuration by 10%. An ideal comparison that ignores ordering is useful only as a performance reference because it is not crash-consistent. The evaluated mechanism requires per-thread buffering, retained versions, dependency metadata, and cache/coherence changes; aggregate chip-area and power costs are not established here. Cross-thread conflicts must still be handled, and conservative dependency tracking can create false positives. The contribution is therefore a workload-informed separation of ordering and completion with demonstrated simulated performance benefits, rather than an assumption that persistence dependencies can be discarded.
